dryRun.title: Where should this piece of state live?
rows: selected filter shared by list + chart
dryRun.note: Start local. Lift state to the closest common parent when siblings need it. Use context for rarely-changing app-wide values, a server-cache library for server data, and a store for complex client state shared widely. Also: never store what you can derive.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
function Celsius({ c, onC }) { return <input value={c} onChange={(e) => onC(e.target.value)} /> }
function Show({ c }) { return <p>{c === '' ? '' : (c * 9) / 5 + 32}</p> }
function App() { const [c, setC] = useState(''); return <><Celsius c={c} onC={setC} /><Show c={c} /></> }
why: State lifted to App, passed down to both children: the input writes it, the display reads it.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
function List({ items }) { const [count, setCount] = useState(items.length); return <p>{count}</p> }
why: Copying a prop into state freezes it at the first value. Derive it instead: const count = items.length.

think.q: Why not keep API data in Redux by default?
opts: Server data needs caching, refetching, deduping and invalidation: a server-cache library does that for you
why: Client state and server state are different problems.

think.q: Where should "page 3 of search results for shoes" live?
opts: In the URL (search params), so it survives reload and can be shared
why: The URL is state too.

think.q: You store items and itemCount in state. Problem?
opts: They can drift apart; compute the count from items during render
why: One source of truth, derive the rest.

try.task: Lift state up: write Converter() with two inputs labelled "Celsius" and "Fahrenheit". Typing in either updates the other (round to 1 decimal). Keep ONE piece of state (the last edited value and its scale) and derive the other.
try.hint: state = { scale: "c" | "f", value: string }; derive each input's value; empty input → both empty.

takeaway.key: Keep state as local as possible, lift it to the closest common parent, derive everything you can, and use the right tool for server data and global client state.
mistakes: Global stores for state only one component uses.

dryRun.title: One context { cart, dispatch } vs two contexts
dryRun.note: Context is a delivery mechanism, not a state manager. To avoid needless re-renders: memoize the value, split state and dispatch into separate contexts (dispatch never changes), and keep fast-changing values out of widely used contexts.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
const State = createContext(0), Dispatch = createContext(null)
let buttonRenders = 0
const AddButton = memo(function AddButton() { const d = useContext(Dispatch); buttonRenders++; return <button onClick={() => d((n) => n + 1)}>add</button> })
function Badge() { return <b>{useContext(State)}</b> }
function App() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); return <Dispatch value={setN}><State value={n}><Badge /><AddButton /></State></Dispatch> }
why: The badge updates; the button reads only the stable dispatch context, so it never re-renders.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
const Ctx = createContext(null)
let buttonRenders = 0
const AddButton = memo(function AddButton() { const { setN } = useContext(Ctx); buttonRenders++; return <button onClick={() => setN((n) => n + 1)}>add</button> })
function App() { const [n, setN] = useState(0); return <Ctx value={{ n, setN }}><AddButton /></Ctx> }
why: One combined context: every state change creates a new value, so even the button that only needs setN re-renders.

think.q: Why is context alone often not enough for big, frequently changing state?
opts: Every consumer re-renders on every change; there are no selectors
why: Stores like Zustand let components subscribe to slices.

think.q: Which is a great use of context?
opts: A text input's value on every keystroke
Theme, locale, current user, an API client: read often, changed rarely
why: Rarely changing, widely needed.

think.q: What does the default value in createContext(defaultValue) do?
opts: Used only when there is no provider above the consumer
A fallback when value is null
why: Many teams use null and throw in a custom hook instead.

try.task: Write CartProvider using useReducer with two contexts, plus hooks useCart() (items array) and useCartDispatch(). Actions: { type: "add", item } and { type: "clear" }. A component that only uses useCartDispatch must not re-render when items change.
examples: const dispatch = useCartDispatch(); dispatch({ type: "add", item: "pen" })
try.hint: Provide state and dispatch in separate providers; dispatch from useReducer is stable.

takeaway.key: Context delivers values; it does not optimise. Memoize values, split state from dispatch, keep hot state elsewhere.
mistakes: A new object value every render.

dryRun.title: useQuery({ queryKey: ["user", 1], queryFn, staleTime: 60_000 })
rows: no new request: reads the same cache entry (deduped)
shows cached data and refetches in the background
dryRun.note: Server state is a cache of something you do not own. TanStack Query handles caching by key, deduping requests, background refetching, retries, and invalidation after mutations. You describe what to fetch; it decides when.

think.q: Why include the user id in the query key: ["user", id]?
opts: The key identifies the cached data; a different id must be a different cache entry (and refetch)
why: Everything the query depends on goes in the key.

think.q: What is the difference?
opts: staleTime: how long data counts as fresh (no refetch). gcTime: how long unused data stays in memory
why: Default staleTime is 0, so data is "stale" immediately and refetches on mount/focus.

think.q: You add a todo via an API. How do you update the list?
why: Invalidation marks it stale and refetches whatever is on screen.

think.q: What does useEffect + fetch typically miss compared to TanStack Query?
opts: Caching, dedupe, race handling, retries, background refresh, and shared loading state
why: You end up writing a worse version of the library.

think.q: Three components mount at once with the same key. How many requests?
opts: One; they share the in-flight promise
why: Deduping by key is built in.

try.task: Write a tiny query cache: createQueryCache({ now }) with fetchQuery(key, fn, staleTime) that returns a promise of the data: fresh cached data is reused, in-flight requests for the same key are shared, stale data triggers a new fn() call. Also invalidate(key).
examples: two calls at once → getUser called once
try.hint: Map key → { data, updatedAt, promise }. If promise in flight return it; if data and now() - updatedAt < staleTime return Promise.resolve(data).

checks.t: reuses fresh data, refetches stale data
invalidate forces a refetch, errors are not cached

takeaway.key: Server state = a cache keyed by query keys: dedupe, staleTime, background refetch, invalidation after mutations. Use TanStack Query instead of hand-written effects.
mistakes: Missing variables in the query key.

dryRun.title: dispatch({ type: "todos/added", payload: "Learn" })
rows: may log, delay, or dispatch more
saves the new state, notifies subscribers
re-renders components whose selected value changed
dryRun.note: Redux keeps all global client state in one store, changed only by dispatching actions to pure reducers. That makes changes predictable, loggable and time-travel-debuggable. Middleware handles side effects; selectors read slices.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
function createStore(reducer, state) { const subs = new Set(); return { getState: () => state, dispatch: (a) => { state = reducer(state, a); subs.forEach((s) => s()) }, subscribe: (s) => (subs.add(s), () => subs.delete(s)) } }
const store = createStore((s, a) => (a.type === 'inc' ? s + 1 : s), 0)
function Count() { const n = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getState); return <p>{n}</p> }
why: Only "inc" changes state; React subscribes to the store with useSyncExternalStore (what react-redux uses).

think.q: Why must reducers be pure?
opts: So the same actions always produce the same state: replay, time travel and tests all depend on it
Because Redux runs in a worker
why: Side effects go in middleware (thunks, listeners).

think.q: useSelector((s) => s.todos.filter((t) => t.done)) re-renders on every store change. Why?
opts: filter returns a new array each time, so the selected value always looks changed
why: Memoize with createSelector, or select primitive values.

think.q: Where should an API call triggered by an action go?
opts: In a thunk/listener middleware, not in the reducer
why: Reducers compute; middleware does side effects.

think.q: When is Redux a good fit today?
opts: Large apps with lots of shared client state, many contributors, and a need for strict, traceable updates
why: Many apps need just local state + TanStack Query.

try.task: Write the core of Redux: createStore(reducer, preloadedState) with getState, dispatch (returns the action), subscribe (returns unsubscribe; listeners added during a dispatch run next time), and combineReducers(map). Dispatch an init action { type: "@@init" } on creation.
try.hint: combineReducers returns (state = {}, action) => new object with each key's reducer applied; keep the same object if nothing changed.

checks.t: dispatch updates state and notifies until unsubscribed
unknown actions keep the same state object

takeaway.key: Redux = one store, actions describe what happened, pure reducers compute the next state, middleware does side effects, selectors read slices.
mistakes: Selectors that return new objects every time.

dryRun.title: createSlice({ name: "todos", initialState: [], reducers: { added(state, action) { state.push(action.payload) } } })
rows: safe: Immer turns the "mutation" into a new immutable state
store with thunk + dev checks + DevTools, no boilerplate
dryRun.note: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, modern way to write Redux. createSlice generates action creators and the reducer; Immer lets you write "mutating" code safely; configureStore sets up good defaults; RTK Query adds data fetching.

think.q: Inside an RTK reducer, state.items.push(x) is fine. Why?
opts: RTK allows mutation of the real state
Immer records the changes on a draft and produces a new immutable state
why: Outside createSlice/createReducer it would be a real mutation bug.

think.q: In an RTK case reducer, what must you NOT do?
opts: Mutate the draft AND return a new value in the same reducer
why: Either mutate the draft or return a replacement, not both.

think.q: createSlice({ name: "cart", reducers: { removed } }). What is the action type?
why: Types are generated as name/reducerKey.

think.q: Where does RTK put async logic like fetching a user?
opts: createAsyncThunk (pending/fulfilled/rejected actions) or RTK Query endpoints
why: RTK Query is the RTK answer to TanStack Query.

think.q: Is hand-written Redux (switch statements, action type constants) still recommended?
opts: No, the Redux team recommends RTK for all Redux code
why: RTK is less code and safer defaults.

try.task: Write a mini createSlice({ name, initialState, reducers }) (without Immer: case reducers return the new state) returning { name, reducer, actions }. Each action creator makes { type: `${name}/${key}`, payload }; the reducer handles only its own types and starts from initialState.
examples: const s = createSlice({ name: "counter", initialState: 0, reducers: { added: (st, a) => st + a.payload } })
try.hint: Build a Map from full type to case reducer; reducer = (state = initialState, action) => case ? case(state, action) : state.

checks.t: reducer handles its cases from initialState

takeaway.key: RTK = modern Redux: createSlice (actions + reducer, Immer drafts), configureStore defaults, createAsyncThunk / RTK Query for async.
mistakes: Mutating AND returning in one case reducer.
Writing old-style Redux boilerplate in new code.

dryRun.title: const useCart = create((set) => ({ items: [], add: (x) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, x] })) }))
dryRun.note: Zustand is a tiny store: one create() call gives you a hook. Components subscribe through a selector and re-render only when that selected value changes. No providers, no reducers, no boilerplate.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
function create(init) { let state; const subs = new Set(); const set = (fn) => { state = { ...state, ...fn(state) }; subs.forEach((l) => l()) }; state = init(set); const sub = (l) => (subs.add(l), () => subs.delete(l)); const useStore = (sel) => useSyncExternalStore(sub, () => sel(state)); useStore.getState = () => state; return useStore }
const useStore = create((set) => ({ count: 0, other: 0, inc: () => set((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 })), bump: () => set((s) => ({ other: s.other + 1 })) }))
let renders = 0
function Count() { renders++; return <b>{useStore((s) => s.count)}</b> }
why: Changing "other" does not re-render Count, because its selected value (count) did not change. Only inc did.

think.q: const { a, b } = useStore((s) => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b })) causes a render loop warning or extra renders. Why?
opts: a and b must be functions
The selector returns a new object every time; use useShallow or select separately
why: Selectors should return stable values.

think.q: Does Zustand need a Provider at the top of the app?
opts: No, the store is a module-level hook (providers are optional, e.g. for SSR or per-test stores)
why: That is part of why it is so light.

think.q: How do you read or update a Zustand store outside a component (e.g. in an API helper)?
why: Hooks only work in components; getState works anywhere.

think.q: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit for a mid-size app with some shared client state?
opts: Zustand is simpler with less ceremony; RTK gives stricter structure and devtools conventions for larger teams
why: Both are fine; pick based on team and app size.

try.task: Write a mini create(initializer): returns a hook useStore(selector = (s) => s) built on useSyncExternalStore, with useStore.getState() and useStore.setState(partialOrFn) (shallow merge). A component must only re-render when its selected value changes.
examples: const useCounter = create((set) => ({ n: 0, inc: () => set((s) => ({ n: s.n + 1 })) }))
try.hint: Keep state + a Set of listeners; setState merges and notifies; the hook calls useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => selector(state)).

checks.t: getState and setState work outside React
components read and update the store
only re-renders when the selected value changes

takeaway.key: Zustand: create() gives a hook; subscribe with selectors so components re-render only for what they use. getState/setState work outside React.
mistakes: Putting server data in a client store.

problems.name: Build a Mini State Management Library

dryRun.title: const priceAtom = atom(10); const qtyAtom = atom(2); const totalAtom = atom((get) => get(priceAtom) * get(qtyAtom))
rows: recomputed only when price or qty changed
dryRun.note: Atomic state (Jotai, Recoil) builds global state from many tiny atoms. Derived atoms compute from others, and each component subscribes only to the atoms it reads, so updates are precise without writing selectors.

think.q: How is Jotai's model different from one big store?
opts: State is split into many independent atoms; derived atoms depend on others like a spreadsheet
It stores state in the URL
why: Bottom-up instead of top-down.

think.q: A derived atom atom((get) => get(a) + get(b)) recomputes when…
opts: a or b changes (only its dependencies)
why: Dependencies are tracked automatically through get.

think.q: What happened to Recoil?
opts: It is the default React API
It was archived by Meta in 2025; Jotai is the maintained choice for this style
why: Pick maintained libraries.

think.q: Atomic state is a great fit for…
opts: Many small independent pieces of shared state, like editor toolbar options
A single counter in one component
why: Each piece updates on its own.

think.q:
import { useState, useEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, useSyncExternalStore, StrictMode } from 'react'
function atom(v) { const subs = new Set(); return { get: () => v, set: (n) => { v = n; subs.forEach((l) => l()) }, sub: (l) => (subs.add(l), () => subs.delete(l)) } }
const useAtomValue = (a) => useSyncExternalStore(a.sub, a.get)
const a = atom(1), b = atom(1)
let aRenders = 0
function A() { aRenders++; return <i>{useAtomValue(a)}</i> }
function B() { return <b>{useAtomValue(b)}</b> }
why: Only components reading atom b re-render; A never noticed.

try.task: Write atom(initial), computed(fn, deps) (a read-only atom recomputed from dependency atoms) and useAtom(a) returning [value, set] (set is undefined for computed atoms), using useSyncExternalStore.
examples: const price = atom(10), qty = atom(2), total = computed(() => price.get() * qty.get(), [price, qty])
try.hint: atom: { get, set, subscribe }. computed: cache the value, subscribe to each dep and recompute + notify on change.

checks.t: components re-render only for atoms they read

takeaway.key: Atoms are tiny independent pieces of state; derived atoms compute from them; components subscribe to exactly what they read.
